title: Model reduction in time: Learning flow maps for reducing stochastic dynamical systems in time

paper.title: Model reduction in time: Learning flow maps for reducing stochastic dynamical systems in time
paper.abstract: Abstract Predictions with dynamical systems can be computationally expensive—even with reduced models—because reaching future prediction times can require many sequential time integration steps. We propose Flow-Map First-Order Trajectory Matching (FM-FTM), a nonintrusive model reduction approach that accelerates ensemble predictions of stochastic dynamical systems by learning flow maps that replace multiple time-integration steps. Our method uses first-order trajectory matching (FTM) to learn a deterministic representation of the stochastic probability-current dynamics and then reduces its evolution over time into a flow map whose evaluation directly yields predictions over long time horizons. Numerical experiments on evolution problems with stochastic forcing demonstrate that FM-FTM accelerates ensemble predictions by up to two orders of magnitude while accurately predicting time marginals and ensemble statistics.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Ensemble predictions of stochastic and chaotic dynamical systems are essential for uncertainty quantification and probabilistic forecasting. Accurate numerical simulations can generate the trajectories needed for these predictions but the computational costs are often too high when the number of ensemble members is large. Reduced models can decrease the computational costs by restricting the state space of underlying dynamical systems to a lower dimensional subspace [ 65 , 5 , 1 , 3 , 4 , 40 , 41 , 35 ] . However, reducing the dimension of the states reduces the cost per time step but not necessarily the number of time steps. Even when each time step with a reduced dynamical-system model is inexpensive, the sheer number of time steps can still incur high costs. In this work, we reduce the cost of time integration itself by learning a flow map whose evaluation replaces multiple sequential integration steps. We build on first-order trajectory matching (FTM) [ 36 ] , which learns a deterministic velocity field representing the probability-current dynamics of a stochastic process. Rather than sequentially integrating the corresponding dynamical-system model in the online phase, we approximate its evolution via a flow map that directly predicts the state over far time horizons. The learned flow map enables far-horizon predictions without time integration and thus avoids having to make many time integration steps. Reducing the computational cost of time integration has a long history in numerical analysis and model reduction. First, there are time-parallel methods such as parareal [ 47 ] and multigrid reduction in time [ 26 ] , which reduce the wall-clock time of time integration. Related parallel-in-time formulations have also been explored for chaotic turbulent flows [ 72 ] . Other approaches exploit fine- and coarse-scale descriptions to accelerate time integration, including for stochastic ensembles; see, e.g., [ 30 , 37 , 24 ] . Data-driven coarse-graining approaches learn effective evolution equations from simulation data, including equations for probability distributions of stochastic systems [ 2 ] . There also is a body of literature on reducing the costs of time integration of reduced models. The work [ 42 ] proposes an equation-free reduced model that approximates the evolution of proper-orthogonal-decomposition coefficients over a coarse time step using an explicit polynomial map. Temporal forecasting [ 15 ] reduces the cost of solving time-discrete reduced models, while data-driven coarse propagators [ 14 ] accelerate time-parallel integration. Space-time projection methods [ 22 , 21 ] reduce the time-integration costs by approximating the solution in a low-dimensional space-time subspace, rather than reducing only the spatial dimension. Certified and windowed space-time reduced models offer further accelerate for reducing temporal complexity [ 74 , 57 , 69 ] , while some nonintrusive deep-learning reduced models can directly evaluate solutions at selected times [ 27 , 28 ] . Dynamic mode decomposition provides another data-driven approach to temporal prediction, with error estimates for extrapolation in time [ 52 ] and extensions to inhomogeneous dynamical systems [ 53 ] . Closer to our approach is work on flow-map learning, which approximates discrete-time evolution operators directly from trajectory data, for example using residual neural networks [ 61 ] ; see also [ 23 ] for an overview of flow-map learning in this context. The work [ 17 ] provides a broader framework and software tools for data-driven learning of unknown dynamical systems using ideas related to flow maps. Flow maps also have been learned over variable time intervals and with encouraging consistency with the semigroup property during training [ 16 ] . Also with the objective to acclerate time integration, the work [ 51 ] proposes hierarchical time-steppers that learn flow maps over different physical-time intervals and combine them to accelerate long-horizon predictions. The approach [ 51 ] reduces the number of sequential time-stepping evaluations by exploiting learned evolution maps at multiple temporal resolutions. However, these deterministic flow-map approaches do not directly address the additional challenge of preserving probability distributions and statistical quantities of interest (QoIs) when predicting stochastic ensembles. Our approach specifically builds on ideas developed to accelerate sampling in diffusion and flow-based generative models [ 71 , 48 ] . These models generate samples by numerically integrating learned stochastic or deterministic dynamics, which can require many sequential evaluations. Progressive distillation [ 66 ] reduces the number of sampling steps by distilling multiple teacher steps into fewer student steps. Consistency models [ 70 ] learn mappings along generative trajectories that enable sampling with one or a few model evaluations. A building block for our work is flow-map matching [ 8 ] and related MeanFlow and flow-map self-distillation [ 31 , 9 ] , which learns the flow maps associated with generative velocity fields, including through distillation of a learned velocity model. Together, these methods demonstrate that flow maps can replace numerical integration of learned velocity fields with substantially fewer evaluations. While the generative approaches above reduce integration in artificial sampling time, our focus is on evolution in the physical time of a dynamical system. Figure 1 : While FTM quickly loses accuracy at coarse time steps, FM-FTM maintains accurate predictions by taking far-horizon time jumps, replacing many sequential integration steps with a single flow-map evaluation and thereby accelerating ensemble prediction. Flow maps have also been learned for stochastic systems in physical time. The authors of [ 19 ] combine deterministic and generative stochastic components to learn fixed-step stochastic transitions, while the work [ 50 ] learns such transitions using supervised data generated by a reverse probability-flow ordinary differential equation (ODE). Both approaches generate long-horizon predictions through repeated applications of a learned stochastic map, in contrast to our work that requires a single neural-network evaluation per long-horizon prediction. There are data-driven approach that capture time-marginal dynamics and require only a single neural-network evaluation per time step [ 55 , 6 , 7 , 67 ] , in contrast to traditional auto-regressive diffusion- and flow-based models [ 18 , 13 , 39 ] . Other data-driven approaches have enabled large physical-time steps in stochastic simulation by inferring numerical integrators adapted to coarse time steps [ 45 , 44 ] or learning conditional stochastic collocation points for Monte Carlo sampling [ 49 ] . There is also work on conditional normalizing flows, which have been used to directly sample stochastic states at prescribed physical times without intermediate time integration [ 73 ] . In contrast, our approach learns a single variable-horizon flow map that transports stochastic ensembles between arbitrary pairs of physical times without modeling the full stochastic transition law. We approach the learning of flow maps for ensemble prediction in two stages. First, we use FTM to learn a deterministic dynamical-system model that mimics the stochastic dynamics in the sense that it preserves the time marginals and local probability mass transport. Second, we approximate the evolution of the resulting deterministic dynamical system with a flow map, which leads to our approach called Flow-Map FTM (FM-FTM). This separates the representation of stochastic dynamics from the reduction of their computational cost in time. Unlike conventional coarse time-steppers with a fixed step size, our FM-FTM can predict the ensemble evolution over different time horizons. Thus, the temporal resolution in the online phase is not restricted to a prescribed coarse time step. Furthermore, FM-FTM is nonintrusive in the sense that it requires only trajectory data and no access to the governing equations or corresponding discretized operators. In this respect, it follows the broader and long line of nonintrusive model reduction works; see, e.g., [ 59 , 32 , 62 , 60 , 54 , 46 , 27 , 33 , 63 , 40 , 25 ] . Our numerical results show that the learned flow maps accelerate ensemble predictions by at least one order of magnitude while accurately predicting ensemble statistics and QoIs that depend on the probability current of the stochastic process.

sections.heading: 2.2 Problem formulation
sections.text: We seek to rapidly generate ensembles to estimate QoIs as well as statistics of the distributions ρ ⁡ ( t ) \rho(t) at selected prediction times. Generating an ensemble by time stepping a dynamical model with a fixed integration time step h > 0 h>0 up to time T T requires at least T / h T/h sequential steps, which typically incurs at least T / h T/h many function evaluations. This applies both to the numerical simulation of ( 2 ), when its coefficients are available, and to dynamical models learned from data. These intermediate steps are required by the integrator even when predictions are requested only at times separated by intervals of length τ ≫ h \tau\gg h as shown in Figure 1 . A reduced dynamical model or learned surrogate can lower the cost of each time step but does typically not reduce the number of steps. Our objective is to advance ensembles over horizons τ ≫ h \tau\gg h without carrying out all the intermediate time integration steps, while retaining accurate statistical estimates of interest. We thus target reducing the number of sequential time steps required for ensemble prediction, rather than only the cost per time step.

sections.heading: 3 Flow maps for first-order trajectory matching
sections.text: We aim to learn the effect of time integration once and reuse it for subsequent ensemble predictions to jump over large time horizons τ ≫ h \tau\gg h , instead of performing many small time steps h h . For the stochastic systems considered here, our construction first obtains a deterministic model of the ensemble evolution. We build on the probability-current velocity, which describes the local transport of probability mass through state space [ 56 , 20 , 58 ] . In particular, we learn the probability-current velocity with FTM from the training data ( 1 ) as in [ 36 ] . We then learn the corresponding flow map, which assigns a state x x at time t t to the state reached at time t + τ t+\tau under the deterministic model. Once learned, one flow map evaluation can jump over time horizons τ ≫ h \tau\gg h , without integrating through the intermediate times.

sections.heading: 3.5 Quantities of interest
sections.text: We consider two types of QoIs for stochastic ensemble prediction. First, QoIs that are ensemble averages of functions of the state and depend only on the time marginals ρ ⁡ ( t ) \rho(t) . Second, we consider probability-current QoIs that characterize the local transport of probability mass through state space. Such current-like observables arise naturally in stochastic thermodynamics, where they are used to characterize nonequilibrium transport and dissipation [ 68 , 43 , 29 , 11 , 12 ] . Let ϕ : [ 0 , T ] × ℝ d → ℝ d \phi:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be a smooth test function. We define the time-averaged probability-current QoI as Q ϕ = 1 T ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ∫ 0 T ϕ ​ ( t , X ⁡ ( t ) ) ⊤ ∘ d ​ X ​ ( t ) ] , Q_{\phi}=\frac{1}{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\phi(t,X(t))^{\top}\circ\mathrm{d}X(t)\right], (11) where ∘ \circ denotes Stratonovich integration. In terms of the probability-current velocity, this quantity can equivalently be written as Q ϕ = 1 T ​ ∫ 0 T 𝔼 ⁡ [ ϕ ​ ( t , X ⁡ ( t ) ) ⊤ ​ v ​ ( t , X ⁡ ( t ) ) ] ​ 𝑑 t . Q_{\phi}=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\phi(t,X(t))^{\top}v(t,X(t))\right]\mathrm{d}t. (12) Depending on the choice of ϕ \phi , these QoIs describe quantities such as probability fluxes and circulations. The deterministic probability-current dynamics ( 5 ) preserve both the time marginals and probability-current QoIs of the stochastic process. Since the flow map F F represents the evolution of these dynamics, it inherits these properties. FM-FTM approximates the flow map induced by the learned FTM velocity and therefore aims to retain the same QoIs, up to the approximation errors of FTM and flow-map learning. In particular, local probability-current quantities can be estimated from short-horizon flow-map evaluations without integrating the FTM velocity field. sections.heading: 4 Numerical experiments
sections.text: We now demonstrate that FM-FTM removes the need to integrate the FTM velocity through each intermediate time step, enabling predictions over large jump horizons τ \tau . We evaluate FM-FTM on four different experiments, Duffing oscillator, Rayleigh-Bénard convection, stochastic Burgers, and stochastic Navier-Stokes. Our numerical results indicate that FM-FTM preserves time marginals and statistics across tested jump horizons τ \tau while gaining runtime speedups.

sections.heading: 4.3 Duffing oscillator with stochastic forcing

sections.heading: 4.3.1 Duffing oscillator: Setup, training data, and evaluation metrics

sections.heading: 4.3.2 Duffing oscillator: Results
sections.text: Figure 2 compares the reference distribution, FTM evaluated with a coarse integration step 0.25 0.25 , and FM-FTM evaluated with jump horizons τ = 0.25 \tau=0.25 and τ = 4.0 \tau=4.0 at t = 4 , 8 , 12 t=4,8,12 . Figure 3 quantifies the time-marginal accuracy. FM-FTM achieves errors comparable to FTM integrated with step size h = 0.01 h=0.01 , with little sensitivity to the jump horizon across τ ∈ { 0.5 , 1.0 , 2.0 , 4.0 } \tau\in\{0.5,1.0,2.0,4.0\} . sections.heading: 4.4 Rayleigh-Bénard convection with stochastic forcing
sections.text: We now consider the stochastically forced nine-dimensional model of Rayleigh-Bénard convection introduced in [ 64 ] . The underlying deterministic dynamics exhibit chaotic behavior, providing a more challenging setting for ensemble prediction.

sections.heading: 4.4.1 Rayleigh-Bénard: Setup, training data, and evaluation metrics
sections.text: We consider the nine-dimensional system governed by d ​ X ​ ( t ) = f μ ​ ( X ⁡ ( t ) ) ​ d ​ t + σ ​ d ​ W ​ ( t ) , \mathrm{d}X(t)=f_{\mu}(X(t))\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma\,\mathrm{d}W(t), where f μ : ℝ 9 → ℝ 9 f_{\mu}:\mathbb{R}^{9}\to\mathbb{R}^{9} is the deterministic Rayleigh-Bénard convection vector field given in [ 64 ] and μ \mu is the Rayleigh-type control parameter. We use μ = 13.65 \mu=13.65 , and σ = 0.05 \sigma=0.05 . For the training data, we generate N = 20000 N=20000 trajectories with initial conditions drawn from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , ( 0.02 ) 2 ​ I 9 ) \mathcal{N}(0,(0.02)^{2}I_{9}) , integrated with the Euler-Maruyama scheme using reference integration step size h ref = 0.01 h_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.01 over time interval [ 0 , 20 ] [0,20] . For ensemble prediction with FTM, we integrate v θ v_{\theta} using step size h = h ref h=h_{\text{ref}} . The flow map F ψ F_{\psi} is parametrized as an MLP with 6 layers and hidden dimension 512, with ReLU activations. sections.heading: 4.5 Stochastically forced Burgers equation
sections.text: We now consider the one-dimensional Burgers equation with stochastic forcing to evaluate FM-FTM for spatially distributed dynamics. In this setting, we assess whether FM-FTM accurately predicts energy and enstrophy of ensemble members over large jump horizons.

sections.heading: 4.5.3 Burgers: Results
sections.text: Figure 7 shows that FM-FTM accurately predicts ensemble-mean energy across all tested jump horizons τ ∈ { 0.25 , 0.5 , 1.0 } \tau\in\{0.25,0.5,1.0\} . sections.heading: 4.6 Forced turbulence
sections.text: We consider the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with stochastic forcing.

sections.heading: 4.6.2 Turbulence: Evaluation metrics
sections.text: We use 1024 1024 test initial conditions and FM-FTM jump horizons τ ∈ { 0.625 , 1.25 } \tau\in\{0.625,1.25\} . We evaluate the relative errors in ensemble-mean kinetic energy and enstrophy, computed from the velocity and vorticity fields, respectively. We also compare the kinetic-energy spectra at selected times to assess the distribution of energy across spatial scales. To assess computational efficiency, we measure the wall-clock time required to generate trajectories with the reference physics model, FTM, and FM-FTM at the tested jump horizons.

sections.heading: 4.6.3 Forced turbulence: Results
sections.text: Integrating the learned FTM velocity field becomes unstable when the time-step size is increased from h = 0.025 h=0.025 to h = 0.25 h=0.25 , as shown in Figure 1 . In contrast, FM-FTM produces accurate predictions with jump horizon τ = 0.25 \tau=0.25 . Thus, FM-FTM enables rollouts over large jump horizons while maintaining accurate predictions and preserving coherent vorticity structures in this example. Accurate ensemble statistics are retained at even larger jump horizons, as shown in Figure 8 , where FM-FTM accurately predicts kinetic energy and enstrophy across the tested jump horizons τ ∈ { 0.625 , 1.25 } \tau\in\{0.625,1.25\} , with relative errors of similar magnitude to those of FTM over much of the time interval. With τ = 1.25 \tau=1.25 , FM-FTM requires only 20 20 flow-map evaluations over time interval [ 0 , 25 ] [0,25] , compared with 1000 1000 sequential integration steps for FTM using h = 0.025 h=0.025 . Thus, FM-FTM retains accurate predictions of physical ensemble statistics while reducing the number of sequential evaluations by a factor of 50 50 . Figure 9 (right) shows that FM-FTM with τ = 1.25 \tau=1.25 also predicts well the kinetic-energy spectrum at t = 25 t=25 , closely matching the reference across the plotted wavenumbers. This demonstrates that FM-FTM captures not only integrated ensemble statistics but also the distribution of kinetic energy across spatial scales. Figure 9 (left) demonstrates the computational savings. FM-FTM reduces trajectory-generation time by approximately 26 × 26\times and 49 × 49\times relative to FTM for τ = 0.625 \tau=0.625 and τ = 1.25 \tau=1.25 , respectively. Compared with the physics model, FM-FTM with τ = 1.25 \tau=1.25 accelerates predictions by more than two orders of magnitude. These results provide further evidence that FM-FTM reduces the computational cost of ensemble prediction while retaining accurate turbulence statistics.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Our results demonstrate that stochastic ensemble predictions can be accelerated by reducing the dynamics in time, rather than only reducing the state dimension or making individual time steps cheaper. By approximating the evolution of a learned probability-current velocity with a flow map, FM-FTM replaces sequential time integration with evaluations of a learned flow map. Our numerical experiments show that FM-FTM accurately captures time marginals, probability-current quantities, and physical ensemble statistics over time horizons that are orders of magnitude larger than the time-integration step size of the underlying dynamical model. Thus, overall, these results show that the time resolution needed to accurately integrate a dynamical model need not determine the computational cost of predictions when predictions are required only at selected times. This puts model reduction in time, via, e.g., flow-map approximations as in this work, as a complementary approach to model reduction in state space.

We propose Flow-Map First-Order Trajectory Matching (FM-FTM), a nonintrusive model reduction approach that accelerates ensemble predictions of stochastic dynamical systems by learning flow maps that replace multiple time-integration steps. Our method uses first-order trajectory matching (FTM) to learn a deterministic representation of the stochastic probability-current dynamics and then reduces its evolution over time into a flow map whose evaluation directly yields predictions over long time horizons. Numerical experiments on evolution problems with stochastic forcing demonstrate that FM-FTM accelerates ensemble predictions by up to two orders of magnitude while accurately predicting time marginals and ensemble statistics. 1 Introduction Ensemble predictions of stochastic and chaotic dynamical systems are essential for uncertainty quantification and probabilistic forecasting. Accurate numerical simulations can generate the trajectories needed for these predictions but the computational costs are often too high when the number of ensemble members is large. Reduced models can decrease the computational costs by restricting the state space of underlying dynamical systems to a lower dimensional subspace [ 65 , 5 , 1 , 3 , 4 , 40 , 41 , 35 ] . However, reducing the dimension of the states reduces the cost per time step but not necessarily the number of time steps. Even when each time step with a reduced dynamical-system model is inexpensive, the sheer number of time steps can still incur high costs. In this work, we reduce the cost of time integration itself by learning a flow map whose evaluation replaces multiple sequential integration steps. We build on first-order trajectory matching (FTM) [ 36 ] , which learns a deterministic velocity field representing the probability-current dynamics of a stochastic process. Rather than sequentially integrating the corresponding dynamical-system model in the online phase, we approximate its evolution via a flow map that directly predicts the state over far time horizons. The learned flow map enables far-horizon predictions without time integration and thus avoids having to make many time integration steps. Reducing the computational cost of time integration has a long history in numerical analysis and model reduction. First, there are time-parallel methods such as parareal [ 47 ] and multigrid reduction in time [ 26 ] , which reduce the wall-clock time of time integration. Related parallel-in-time formulations have also been explored for chaotic turbulent flows [ 72 ] . Other approaches exploit fine- and coarse-scale descriptions to accelerate time integration, including for stochastic ensembles; see, e.g., [ 30 , 37 , 24 ] . Data-driven coarse-graining approaches learn effective evolution equations from simulation data, including equations for probability distributions of stochastic systems [ 2 ] . There also is a body of literature on reducing the costs of time integration of reduced models. The work [ 42 ] proposes an equation-free reduced model that approximates the evolution of proper-orthogonal-decomposition coefficients over a coarse time step using an explicit polynomial map. Temporal forecasting [ 15 ] reduces the cost of solving time-discrete reduced models, while data-driven coarse propagators [ 14 ] accelerate time-parallel integration. Space-time projection methods [ 22 , 21 ] reduce the time-integration costs by approximating the solution in a low-dimensional space-time subspace, rather than reducing only the spatial dimension. Certified and windowed space-time reduced models offer further accelerate for reducing temporal complexity [ 74 , 57 , 69 ] , while some nonintrusive deep-learning reduced models can directly evaluate solutions at selected times [ 27 , 28 ] . Dynamic mode decomposition provides another data-driven approach to temporal prediction, with error estimates for extrapolation in time [ 52 ] and extensions to inhomogeneous dynamical systems [ 53 ] . Closer to our approach is work on flow-map learning, which approximates discrete-time evolution operators directly from trajectory data, for example using residual neural networks [ 61 ] ; see also [ 23 ] for an overview of flow-map learning in this context. The work [ 17 ] provides a broader framework and software tools for data-driven learning of unknown dynamical systems using ideas related to flow maps. Flow maps also have been learned over variable time intervals and with encouraging consistency with the semigroup property during training [ 16 ] . Also with the objective to acclerate time integration, the work [ 51 ] proposes hierarchical time-steppers that learn flow maps over different physical-time intervals and combine them to accelerate long-horizon predictions. The approach [ 51 ] reduces the number of sequential time-stepping evaluations by exploiting learned evolution maps at multiple temporal resolutions. However, these deterministic flow-map approaches do not directly address the additional challenge of preserving probability distributions and statistical quantities of interest (QoIs) when predicting stochastic ensembles. Our approach specifically builds on ideas developed to accelerate sampling in diffusion and flow-based generative models [ 71 , 48 ] . These models generate samples by numerically integrating learned stochastic or deterministic dynamics, which can require many sequential evaluations. Progressive distillation [ 66 ] reduces the number of sampling steps by distilling multiple teacher steps into fewer student steps. Consistency models [ 70 ] learn mappings along generative trajectories that enable sampling with one or a few model evaluations. A building block for our work is flow-map matching [ 8 ] and related MeanFlow and flow-map self-distillation [ 31 , 9 ] , which learns the flow maps associated with generative velocity fields, including through distillation of a learned velocity model. Together, these methods demonstrate that flow maps can replace numerical integration of learned velocity fields with substantially fewer evaluations. While the generative approaches above reduce integration in artificial sampling time, our focus is on evolution in the physical time of a dynamical system. Figure 1 : While FTM quickly loses accuracy at coarse time steps, FM-FTM maintains accurate predictions by taking far-horizon time jumps, replacing many sequential integration steps with a single flow-map evaluation and thereby accelerating ensemble prediction. Flow maps have also been learned for stochastic systems in physical time. The authors of [ 19 ] combine deterministic and generative stochastic components to learn fixed-step stochastic transitions, while the work [ 50 ] learns such transitions using supervised data generated by a reverse probability-flow ordinary differential equation (ODE). Both approaches generate long-horizon predictions through repeated applications of a learned stochastic map, in contrast to our work that requires a single neural-network evaluation per long-horizon prediction. There are data-driven approach that capture time-marginal dynamics and require only a single neural-network evaluation per time step [ 55 , 6 , 7 , 67 ] , in contrast to traditional auto-regressive diffusion- and flow-based models [ 18 , 13 , 39 ] . Other data-driven approaches have enabled large physical-time steps in stochastic simulation by inferring numerical integrators adapted to coarse time steps [ 45 , 44 ] or learning conditional stochastic collocation points for Monte Carlo sampling [ 49 ] . There is also work on conditional normalizing flows, which have been used to directly sample stochastic states at prescribed physical times without intermediate time integration [ 73 ] . In contrast, our approach learns a single variable-horizon flow map that transports stochastic ensembles between arbitrary pairs of physical times without modeling the full stochastic transition law. We approach the learning of flow maps for ensemble prediction in two stages. First, we use FTM to learn a deterministic dynamical-system model that mimics the stochastic dynamics in the sense that it preserves the time marginals and local probability mass transport. Second, we approximate the evolution of the resulting deterministic dynamical system with a flow map, which leads to our approach called Flow-Map FTM (FM-FTM). This separates the representation of stochastic dynamics from the reduction of their computational cost in time. Unlike conventional coarse time-steppers with a fixed step size, our FM-FTM can predict the ensemble evolution over different time horizons. Thus, the temporal resolution in the online phase is not restricted to a prescribed coarse time step. Furthermore, FM-FTM is nonintrusive in the sense that it requires only trajectory data and no access to the governing equations or corresponding discretized operators. In this respect, it follows the broader and long line of nonintrusive model reduction works; see, e.g., [ 59 , 32 , 62 , 60 , 54 , 46 , 27 , 33 , 63 , 40 , 25 ] . Our numerical results show that the learned flow maps accelerate ensemble predictions by at least one order of magnitude while accurately predicting ensemble statistics and QoIs that depend on the probability current of the stochastic process. 2 Preliminaries and problem formulation We provide preliminaries and state the problem formulation. 2.1 Trajectory data and stochastic dynamics Let ( X ⁡ ( t ) ) t ∈ [ 0 , T ] (X(t))_{t\in[0,T]} be a continuous-time stochastic process with state space ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} . Generating an ensemble by time stepping a dynamical model with a fixed integration time step h > 0 h>0 up to time T T requires at least T / h T/h sequential steps, which typically incurs at least T / h T/h many function evaluations. This applies both to the numerical simulation of ( 2 ), when its coefficients are available, and to dynamical models learned from data. These intermediate steps are required by the integrator even when predictions are requested only at times separated by intervals of length τ ≫ h \tau\gg h as shown in Figure 1 . A reduced dynamical model or learned surrogate can lower the cost of each time step but does typically not reduce the number of steps. Our objective is to advance ensembles over horizons τ ≫ h \tau\gg h without carrying out all the intermediate time integration steps, while retaining accurate statistical estimates of interest. We thus target reducing the number of sequential time steps required for ensemble prediction, rather than only the cost per time step. 3 Flow maps for first-order trajectory matching We aim to learn the effect of time integration once and reuse it for subsequent ensemble predictions to jump over large time horizons τ ≫ h \tau\gg h , instead of performing many small time steps h h . For the stochastic systems considered here, our construction first obtains a deterministic model of the ensemble evolution. We build on the probability-current velocity, which describes the local transport of probability mass through state space [ 56 , 20 , 58 ] . In particular, we learn the probability-current velocity with FTM from the training data ( 1 ) as in [ 36 ] . We then learn the corresponding flow map, which assigns a state x x at time t t to the state reached at time t + τ t+\tau under the deterministic model.
